Linea Directa Aseguradora (LDA-ES): a good business at a cheap price with a timing problem, because FY27 earnings stall about 6% below consensus before compounding resumes

Written 8 November 2026 for Richard. Share price EUR 1.226 (23 October 2026); market value about EUR 1.34bn on 1,088.4m shares. "We" and "our" refer to the Financial Analyst's forecasts (see the end notes).

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line for Richard

Linea Directa is a good business at a cheap price, but the next twelve months work against a buyer. The model's base return to December 2027 is +21.6%, almost all from earnings and dividends. Weighted for a negative skew in FY27, the expected return falls to about +10%. The practical answer is to stage the position rather than take it whole:

  1. The better entry point is more likely after the Q1 27 results (late April 2027) or the H1 27 results (late July 2027), when FY27 consensus will have been cut towards our numbers.
  2. Three dated events could make the risk/reward unusually positive sooner: a payout policy of 70% or more in late February, a Mutua Madrileña retreat from its tariff freeze in March, and a Q1 27 print showing a 3% written motor price with a flat loss ratio.
  3. The case against Linea Directa is bounded: the downside case (about -30% to December 2027) is dated and starts from a far stronger position than the 2022 to 2023 loss.

The company. Linea Directa is Spain's only listed pure direct insurer. Motor insurance is 81% of its EUR 1.13bn of premiums, home insurance 15% and health insurance 3%. Linea Directa sells only by phone, web and app from one site in Madrid; it has no brokers, no branches and no debt, and it owns its repair centres. Bankinter spun Linea Directa out in 2021, and two linked shareholder blocks, Cartival (about 20.7%) and Bankinter (17.4%), together hold 38% of the shares.

The recent history. The 2022 to 2023 claims-inflation shock raised Linea Directa's combined ratio (CR: claims plus expenses as a share of earned premium) from about 90% to 104% and pushed the company into a loss. The sector's fastest repricing then brought the CR back to 91.3% for the nine months to September 2026, and nine-month net income rose 35% to EUR 80.4m.

The case in one paragraph
Linea Directa has finished its margin recovery and now runs a growth strategy. The company raises motor prices by about 1.5% a year while the market raises them by 4% to 6%, and its expense ratio, 7 to 8 points below competitors', pays for that price gap. The result is share gain: Linea Directa's premiums grew 8.9% against a market growing about 6%. Our model therefore compounds premium volume at about 7% a year, holds the CR in a 91% to 92% band, raises the payout from 53% to 70% as growth slows, and grows EPS by about 7.7% a year from FY25 to FY30. That describes a cheap, high-return (ROE 23% to 25%), self-funding and predictable business. The obstacle to a straightforward purchase today is FY27. The low prices Linea Directa wrote in 2026 earn through in 2027 while claims costs rise 3.5% to 4.5%, so FY27 net income is flat (EUR 106m against EUR 105.5m in FY26) and about 6% below a consensus that still carries the H1 26 margin into 2027. The company will meet its "low 90s" CR guidance; it will not meet consensus.

The eight insights that matter

1

Linea Directa's current combined ratio is a plateau below its own history, not a margin peak. The improvement in the H1 26 CR came from home weather and health. The motor loss ratio was flat (72.9% against 72.8%), and in Q3 it was flat to 0.25 points better once Q3 25's severe claims are excluded. Motor, 81% of the book, is therefore holding its margin, not improving it. The market calls a 91% CR a "margin peak", but Linea Directa's own CR was 86% to 88% before 2022, so 91% is a plateau 4 to 6 points worse than history. The model's FY30 net income (EUR 124m) is still below FY20's EUR 135m, on 70% more revenue. This reframing is the strongest positive in the case that the market has not articulated.

2

The FY27 profit air pocket is arithmetic, not a crisis. The 1% to 2% motor price increases written in 2026 fix the price that Linea Directa earns in 2027. Claims cost per policy rises 3.5% to 4.5% in 2027: the Baremo (Spain's statutory scale for bodily-injury compensation) rises 3.3% to 3.5%, spare parts 5.1% and repair labour 3.7%. The home CR reverts from 86.8% towards the 90% to 91% that the CFO calls "normal". The group CR therefore rises to 92.0% from about 91.3%, FY27 net income is flat, and we expect consensus to be cut by 4% to 8% between February and October 2027.

3

The feared Baremo tail risk has closed. The 2027 Baremo scale rises in line with the pension revaluation (average CPI from December to November), which gives a preliminary 3.33% against market fears of 4% or more; the government confirms the figure on 15 December. The risk that the market narrative still treats as open is therefore nearly known, and benign. The remaining Baremo tail risk has moved to the 2028 update, which 2027 inflation will set (Bank of Spain forecast: 3.7%).

4

Linea Directa's revenue is one of the most forecastable lines in European non-life insurance; its margin is not. Compulsory annual contracts, a six-month lag between written and earned premium, and the trade-off between price and volume keep written premium growth in a 6% to 8% band whatever management does. All the forecasting uncertainty sits in one ratio: 1 point of CR is EUR 9.6m of net income, or 9% of EPS.

5

The FY27 earnings skew is negative, at -17% to +11% around the base case. Two features cause the skew: claims severity hits results within a quarter while repricing takes two to four quarters, and the strategy spends any margin upside on lower prices. Management holds two buffers that make the reported CR stickier than the underlying CR: about 1 to 1.5 points of discretionary marketing spend, and reserve prudence. The first visible sign of stress will therefore be slowing policy growth alongside a falling expense ratio, not a rising CR.

6

Capital is the quiet positive, but solvency caps it. Slowing growth frees capital for a higher payout, because each point of premium growth consumes about EUR 4.7m of own funds a year; the yield on the model's dividends rises from 4.7% (FY26) to 6.1% (FY28). However, a EUR 27m mark-down on bonds in Q3 took the solvency ratio to 191.5%. After the final dividend the ratio sits at about 180% to 185%, the board's dividend reference, plus about 3 points from the January 2027 Solvency II revision. That leaves no room for a buyback.

7

On our earnings, the stock already trades at the guideline fair multiple. The two-year-forward P/E on our earnings is 12.2x, against the 12.38x guideline. The model's +21.6% return to December 2027 therefore splits into 11 points from earnings, 8.8 points from dividends and 1.6 points from the multiple. This is a growth-plus-yield return, not a re-rating story. A re-rating needs either the retail property and casualty (P&C) insurer cohort to recover (Admiral, Tryg and Sampo all sit at the 4th to 9th percentiles of their own ranges) or Linea Directa to close its own 2-to-3-turn discount to that cohort.

8

The sequence of news matters more than the destination. The news flow is favourable to February 2027 (an FY26 beat of about 2%, Baremo relief, a higher dividend, a solvency uplift). It is unfavourable from April to October 2027 (the first year-on-year CR deterioration since 2023, consensus cuts, Mutua Madrileña's 2027 pricing stance). It turns favourable again from 2028 (repricing earned through, health near breakeven, a 70% payout). The attractive entry point is therefore more likely after the Q1 27 or H1 27 results than before them, unless February's capital statement or a Mutua retreat changes the order.

The risk/reward is not yet unusually skewed to the positive; three dated events could make it so.

Each of the three triggers below is plausible and none is signalled. The payout policy and the Q1 27 result cannot be known before late February and late April 2027. Mutua's retreat is more likely than the market assumes, because Mutua's 97% CR ceiling leaves it only 1 to 2 points of room against claims severity of 3.5% or more. Until the triggers arrive, the fundamental outcomes are modestly skewed down, and sell-side revisions are more likely to be cuts than raises.

Late February 2027Linea Directa announces a payout policy of 70% or more of the parent company's profit
March 2027Mutua Madrileña retreats from its tariff freeze on 50% of its motor book
Late April 2027Q1 27 shows a 3% written motor price, a flat loss ratio and 5% policy growth

The five judgements that move the shares most over one to two years, with the arithmetic

The FY27 base case is earned premium of EUR 1,275m, a CR of 92.0%, pre-tax profit of EUR 141.6m, net income of EUR 106.2m and EPS of EUR 0.098 (25% tax rate; 1,088.4m shares). Every judgement below is sized against that base.

Judgement 1: the 2027 motor price-cost scissors. The base case adds 0.5 point to the motor CR, net of the benefit of slower growth (new policies run worse than renewals).

  • Downside: the CR is 1.8 points worse, at a group CR of 93.8%. This happens if CPI stays at 4% to 5%, parts inflation runs at 5% to 6%, Mutua extends its freeze and Linea Directa's repricing lags by four quarters. Pre-tax profit falls by EUR 23.0m to EUR 118.6m, net income is EUR 89m and EPS is EUR 0.082 (-16%). The dividend at a 65% payout is EUR 0.053 instead of EUR 0.063, and solvency drifts to about 178%. At the trough multiple of 9.5x to 10x, the shares would be worth EUR 0.78 to 0.82 (-33% to -37%).
  • Upside: the CR is 1 point better, at a group CR of 91.0%. This happens with benign claims frequency, a third benign weather year and Mutua narrowing its freeze. Pre-tax profit is EUR 154.4m, net income EUR 116m and EPS EUR 0.106 (+9%). At the guideline 12.38x on the resulting two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 0.12, the shares would be worth EUR 1.49 before dividends (+21%).
  • The downside sits further from the base case than the upside does, and that asymmetry is the defining feature of the case.

Judgement 2: home weather. The base case reverts the home CR from 86.8% to 89.5% on about EUR 175m of earned premium; 1 point of home CR is EUR 1.75m of pre-tax profit.

  • A 2023-type weather year (home CR 95.8%) adds 6.3 points to the home CR. That costs EUR 11m pre-tax, EUR 8.3m net and EUR 0.0076 of EPS (-8%).
  • A third benign weather year (home CR 87%) removes 2.5 points from the home CR. That adds EUR 4.4m pre-tax, EUR 3.3m net and EUR 0.003 of EPS (+3%).

Judgement 3: reserve adequacy. The base case assumes zero prior-year reserve development.

Linea Directa's individual accounts under Spanish accounting rules show a 2025 surplus of EUR 33.5m on the run-off of prior-year reserves (about 3.1 points of earned premium), after a 2024 deficit of EUR 25.6m (2.6 points). Motor third-party liability alone swung from an EUR 18.3m deficit to an EUR 15.9m surplus. The company does not disclose how much of that swing reached the IFRS 17 combined ratio.

  • Downside: a precautionary reserve strengthening of 2 to 3 points ahead of the 2028 Baremo, of the kind Mapfre made in Q3 2026, would cost EUR 25m to 38m pre-tax, EUR 19m to 29m net and EUR 0.018 to 0.026 of EPS (-18% to -27%).
  • Upside: a repeat of the 2025 surplus is the mirror image, adding 18% to 27% to EPS.
  • Reserves are the widest single lever on FY27 earnings and the least visible one. That is why the reserving risk adjustment, now set at the 85th percentile of the reserve distribution (Admiral: 94th), belongs on the watch list.

Judgement 4: volume under the Mutua price umbrella. The base case has FY27 written premiums growing 7.0% and policies 4.8%.

  • Suppose Linea Directa's price gap to the market narrows by 2 to 3 points, because Mutua extends its freeze while Linea Directa reprices by 3%. Policy growth then falls to 2% to 3%, written premium growth to about 5%, and written premiums to EUR 1,291m rather than EUR 1,316m. Because premiums earn over the following year, the FY27 profit effect is only about EUR 1m pre-tax. The FY28 effect is about EUR 5m pre-tax (EUR 30m less earned premium at an 8% technical margin, plus 0.2 point of lost expense leverage), EUR 4m net and -3.5% of EPS.
  • The effect of lower volume on earnings is small; its effect on the multiple is not. The market's warning line is Linea Directa's motor growth falling below 7% while Mutua grows at double digits. If investors conclude that the price umbrella is closing, the stock would plausibly lose a turn of multiple (-9%). Volume matters more for the stock's rating than for its profit.

Judgement 5: capital return and the multiple. The base case pays out 60%, 65% and 70% of net income in FY26 to FY28 and holds the two-year-forward multiple at 12.38x.

  • If the payout stays at 55% throughout, dividends per share are EUR 0.053, 0.054 and 0.059 instead of EUR 0.058, 0.063 and 0.075. That removes about 1 point from the return to December 2027 and 3 points from the return to June 2029. A payout policy of 70% or more from FY26 adds about 1 point, and lets the dividend story lead the earnings story.
  • Each turn of multiple on the December 2027 two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 0.112 is worth EUR 0.11 a share, or 9% of today's price. Closing half the discount to the retail P&C cohort (a multiple of 13.0x to 13.5x) is worth +5% to +10%. A stalled CR that takes the multiple back to the 10x to 11x the market paid in 2022 and December 2025 is worth -10% to -18%, before any cut to earnings.

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

The external environment lifts Linea Directa's volume but squeezes its 2027 margin, and the next external threat, a soft market, now looks likely to arrive from 2028, earlier than the model assumed.

Market growth is mostly price. Spanish non-life premiums grew 7.8% in 2025 and slowed to about 5.5% in H1 26; motor premiums grew 6.1% over the first nine months of 2026. The vehicle fleet grew only 2.3%, so most of that growth is price.

Spain combines strong growth with high inflation. Spain is Europe's growth outperformer (GDP growth of 2.3% to 2.4% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027; employment +1.9%), but it is also Europe's inflation outlier (CPI of 4.9% in September and October, led by energy, with Brent crude at about USD 90 to 111 a barrel).

Claims costs are rising faster than Linea Directa's prices. Spare parts cost 5.1% more and repair and maintenance 3.7% more than a year ago (Jefferies' index, September), and electric-vehicle repairs cost 15% to 24% more than conventional ones. Bodily injury is about 30% of motor claims cost, and insurers pay open claims at the Baremo scale of the year of payment. The pension formula sets the 2027 Baremo increase at about 3.3% to 3.5%, up from 2.7% but far below 2023's 8.5%.

The incumbents are still raising prices, except Mutua Madrileña.

Regulation and reinsurance matter little. Regulation is a small net positive for capital: the Solvency II revision from 30 January 2027 releases about EUR 7m of own funds, worth about 3 points of solvency. Regulation is a small negative for costs, through the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, the EU AI Act and sustainability reporting. Reinsurance is cheaper, but Linea Directa buys little of it.

Two sector narratives weigh on all motor insurers. The market fears AI shopping agents (Nordic P&C shares fell 6.9% in three months; DNB Carnegie puts 3% to 15% of EPS at risk) and autonomous vehicles (Admiral has de-rated 45% against the sector). Both fears play out in a risk-off market that sells small, illiquid stocks such as Linea Directa.

Inference: a maturing tailwind is turning into a dated, bounded headwind. The tailwind is the incumbents' price umbrella, under which a low-cost direct insurer wins customers. The umbrella is intact but no longer widening. Mapfre has finished its clean-up and says it will move to premium and unit growth in 2027 to 2029; AXA targets more than 10% a year of direct growth in Spain; and Linea Directa's management said in October that customer acquisition had "slowed slightly" because of competition. The headwind is claims severity running above Linea Directa's own pricing, and it is now mostly quantified. The 2027 Baremo is known to within 0.2 points, and parts and labour costs are running at 4% to 5%. Together they produce the 3.5% to 4.5% growth in claims cost per policy in the model, against an earned price increase of about 2%.

The mechanism the market has not put together: inflation acts on Linea Directa through two channels with different lags. Inflation hurts Linea Directa's margin within a quarter, through claims severity. Inflation helps Linea Directa's volume for a year or more, because incumbents raise prices, Mutua is pushed towards its 97% CR ceiling and the price umbrella widens. The 2027 starting position also differs from 2022's. In 2022 the whole market priced late and Linea Directa had no cost cushion; in 2027 the market is already raising prices by 4% to 6%, and Linea Directa starts from a 91.3% CR with a 20% expense ratio. The dangerous environment for Linea Directa is therefore not inflation but the soft market that follows a margin recovery, when incumbents stop raising prices and chase volume back. The UK motor market did exactly this in 2025 and now expects a 107% motor CR for 2026. The first dated signals of a Spanish soft phase, Mapfre's and AXA's 2027 plans, have just arrived, a year earlier than the margin drift that the model assumed for FY29 to FY30.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market ranks the external risks as Mutua first, the Baremo second and AI agents third. We rank them differently. The Baremo is a dated relief on 15 December. Mutua is fully priced as a threat, and inflation puts Mutua under more pressure than the market narrative allows. The real medium-term risk is the incumbents' turn to volume in 2027 to 2029: that turn is written in Mapfre's and AXA's own documents, and nobody has yet connected it to Linea Directa.

Strongest counter-case. Spanish CPI stays at 4% to 5% through H1 27, Mutua extends its freeze into 2027 because its 297% solvency makes the freeze affordable, and parts inflation runs at 5% to 6%. Three of the six conditions for the downside case have moved closer since October. What would change our view: a 15 December Baremo increase above 3.8%, which would need November CPI far above 5%; or a March 2027 announcement by Mutua extending its freeze through 2027 on 50% or more of its book while Linea Directa's derived motor price increase is still only about 1% to 2%.

Conclusion: the environment is mildly favourable for Linea Directa's volume and mildly unfavourable for its 2027 margin. The worst external tail risk (a Baremo increase of 4% or more) has now closed, and the next one (a soft market from 2028) is arriving earlier than modelled.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. The external forces roughly cancel and tilt slightly negative over two to three years. The incumbents' price umbrella (market motor price +4% to 6%, non-life premiums +5.5% to 6%, Spanish GDP 2%+) lifts volume, but claims-cost growth of 3.5% to 4.5% (Baremo 3.3% to 3.5%, parts +5.1%), Mutua's open-ended tariff freeze, and Mapfre's and AXA's turn to volume from 2027 squeeze the 2027 margin and bring a soft-market risk forward to 2028. The 78th-percentile consensus sales growth is mostly price inflation, and the 2022 to 2023 loss shows how a severity step lands. This is a touch below the External change forces group's 50 because the soft-market threat now falls inside the window, and it sits between Kerry's neutral environment and Indutrade's soft backdrop.

#2 Internally driven corporate change

Management executes one programme well, but the programme's next levers, capital return and disclosure, are in management's gift and unused.

The positives: the same team, the same programme, strong delivery. CEO Patricia Ayuela was re-elected for four years in April 2026, and CFO Carlos Rodríguez-Ugarte fronts the results. The priority inside the programme has shifted from restoring the margin (2023 to 2024: the sector's largest price rises and a deliberate loss of 4.2% to 4.5% of customers) to profitable volume (2025 to 2026: "we do not need to deteriorate combined ratios to drive commercial volume growth").

  • Expense ratio: 22.1% (FY24), 21.1% (FY25), 20.0% (nine months 2026) and 19.4% (Q3 26); motor 18.0%.
  • Headcount down while customers rose 7%; AI resolves about two-thirds of chat queries; fully digital sales are 12% of sales.
  • Solvency rebuilt from the 2023 dividend suspension to 191.5%.
  • Dividend back to EUR 45m for FY25 (70% of the parent company's individual profit, the basis the company uses); the first FY26 interim dividend 20% higher.
  • Guidance raised twice in words in 2026: "comfortable with 92% to 93%" in February, "low 90s" in April.
  • Health, the one loss-making line (CR 125% to 122%; a nine-month technical loss of EUR 4.1m), moves to a new provider network from Q1 2027 (HNA, with 56,500 points of care).
  • Cartival has been adding to its stake (now 20.75%); Bankinter is passive and says it will keep its 17.4%.

The negatives cluster in incentives, controls and access.

  • Annual incentives weight written premiums at 70%; the long-term plan weights premium growth against the sector at 40% and the average CR at 50%.
  • The reserving risk adjustment was lowered from the 95th percentile (2023) to the 85th.
  • Internal control weaknesses rose from 28% to 37% of evaluated systems, with 12 unresolved.
  • The CEO does not take analysts' questions, and the H1 26 call dropped public questions and answers.
  • CEO pay rose about 31% in 2025, while her own shareholding is nominal.
  • A board seat is vacant.
  • EUR 4.6m a year of mediation commissions flow to Bankinter companies.

Inference: the internal change force is real, well funded and consistently executed, but narrow. Linea Directa has no new lever comparable to the 2023 to 2024 repricing. The next levers are capital return and disclosure, and management controls both but has signalled neither: a payout range on the parent company's profit; disclosure of written price, claims frequency, claims severity and reserve development; and an investor event led by the CEO. These are the cheapest re-rating catalysts available for a stock at the 10th percentile of its valuation range with only five or six covering brokers.

So-what for the case: the base case needs Linea Directa to keep doing what it has done for eight quarters. About four-fifths of the expected change rests on strengths the company has already demonstrated. The remaining fifth is where the FY27 risk sits: repricing motor by 3% to 4% into Mutua's freeze without losing policies; reaching breakeven in health under an untested network; and running a reserve buffer at the 85th percentile through a Baremo step. The incentive structure also predicts management's behaviour: management will choose volume over margin whenever the CR allows. That is why the model holds the CR in a band rather than letting it fall towards Q2 26's 90.6%.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market reads the expense leverage Linea Directa has retained (an expense ratio of 19.4% in Q3) as efficiency; we read it as a buffer the company has not yet needed to spend. The market does not model a payout step; we model payouts of 60%, 65% and 70% for FY26 to FY28. We have dropped our earlier idea of a EUR 50m buyback, for two reasons: solvency sits at the 180% reference after the planned dividend, and Cartival needs cash dividends (Cartival received EUR 129m from Bankinter and Linea Directa in 2025 to fund EUR 40m of family distributions).

Strongest counter-case. Linea Directa could be a "false friend": premium growth bought with prices rising more slowly than inflation and flattered by undisclosed reserve releases, which the company's disclosure cannot refute. What would change our view: disclosure in the March 2027 accounts of a 2026 deficit on prior-year reserves; or a Q1 27 expense ratio below 19%, beyond the seasonal effect, while policy additions fall below 30,000 a quarter, which would signal a defensive spending cut rather than efficiency.

Conclusion: a capable operating team is executing one programme well, but the programme's change force is narrowing from operations to capital and disclosure, where management has so far chosen to do nothing.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. The internal change is a continuing, well-executed but narrowing programme. The expense ratio fell from 22.1% to 19.4%, solvency was rebuilt to 191.5%, the dividend was restored and raised, guidance was raised twice in words and health moves to a new network in 2027. But there is no new lever, the next one (capital policy and disclosure) is unused, and incentives favour volume over margin, the reserve buffer has been lowered from the 95th to the 85th percentile and control weaknesses are rising. Profit growth of 35% this year is the end of the repricing recovery, not a new force. This is Richard's 'gently positive but mediocre' case (CVS 55), coherent with the group's 53, and it sits between Shell's incremental self-help and Hexatronic.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Industry structureModerately supportive
Business modelOne strong advantage
Financial profileAbove average
ManagementGood operators, not owners

Industry structure: moderately supportive, but dependent on the two leaders. The top five non-life groups hold 48% of the Spanish market. The Herfindahl concentration index for motor is 651, between the fragmented UK (209) and oligopolistic Italy (979). Motor third-party cover is compulsory, Solvency II and licensing are high barriers, and entry has been negligible for a decade: Admiral Seguros, in Spain since 2006, has 0.46m customers and makes losses, and Verti runs at a 102.6% CR. The Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros, a state-backed pool, absorbs about 95% of extreme-weather losses.

Pricing discipline in Spanish motor insurance depends on the two leaders. When Mapfre and Mutua both raised prices (2024 to early 2025), the market followed; since Mutua chose customer retention over margin, discipline has weakened at the edge. The industry also tolerated poor returns for years: average motor premiums in 2022 were at 2015 levels, and the sector's motor CR was about 98% in 2025. Discipline is therefore recent and unproven through a soft phase.

Linea Directa's channel caps its reach. Brokers and agents control about 70% of Spanish premiums, and the direct and price-comparison channel is thought to top out at 27% to 30% of motor, of which Linea Directa already holds roughly a quarter.

Business model: one strong advantage, several soft ones, and no customer lock-in. The structural advantage is cost. Linea Directa's expense ratio is 20% against Mapfre Iberia's 27.8%, and about 16% to 18% in motor against about 20% for the main competitors. The cost gap lets Linea Directa price about 10% below the industry while earning the best margin in the market (a motor CR of 91.3% for nine months, against 96% at Mapfre Iberia motor and Mutua's 97% ceiling). The model is a "scale economies shared" system: lower cost funds lower prices, lower prices bring volume, and volume spreads the fixed cost of a single site.

The soft advantages are narrowing. They are the brand, which works as a fee for search traffic; pricing agility from data on 2.9m motor risks; and the CAR repair centres with 1,000 partner workshops. Mutua (Akur8 pricing software, EUR 80m of AI spending, the Reynasa parts distributor) and Mapfre (over EUR 1bn a year of technology spending) are digitising fast. Switching costs are low: contracts are annual, comparison sites bring about 30% of direct volume, Linea Directa's net promoter score is 36.8 against Admiral's 50-plus, and retention is about 86% against Mutua's 90%. Linea Directa has an Admiral-type advantage without Admiral's scale or capital-light reinsurance structure. The advantage is sufficient to win share in a disciplined market and to survive a soft one, but not sufficient to justify a moat premium.

Financial profile: above average, clean, but cyclical through the CR. Linea Directa has no debt, and equity of about EUR 440m supports EUR 1.23bn of premiums. Growth needs only about EUR 35m of retained earnings a year, so most profit is distributable. The earnings base is clean (reported profit equals adjusted profit, tax is at the 25% statutory rate, and there is no goodwill), with one exception: the undisclosed contribution of reserve development. Earnings swing with the CR: the pre-tax margin moved from 19.6% (FY20) to -0.7% (FY23) on revenue that changed by only 9%.

Management: good operators, not owner-operators. Management was decisive in the 2023 crisis but late into the 2022 shock. It raises targets only after delivery and is prudent on capital. It is thin on disclosure and investor access, and passive on capital allocation (no buyback at a 10th-percentile multiple). Two linked controlling shareholders shape governance. Management's ambition is the right size for a EUR 1.1bn single-country insurer, and no larger.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market treats Linea Directa as "shoppable earnings behind a mutual price-setter", which is fair, and prices the stock below the retail P&C cohort for its size, its small free float and the memory of 2023. We add that in the Spanish motor market the cost gap decides who grows and who survives a soft phase, and Linea Directa's cost gap has held through a full cycle; the market gives no credit for that survivorship. We agree with the market that there is no moat premium to pay.

Strongest counter-case. AI agents and comparison sites turn the insurer into a commodity behind an interface it does not own, acquisition costs rise for all direct insurers, and the brand-based part of retention erodes. Linea Directa would then have to spend its cost advantage on defending volume rather than on earning a margin. That fragility runs over three to five years, not 18 months. What would change our view: evidence of acquisition-cost inflation (marketing rising above 5% of premiums), or a sustained fall in net customer additions below about 100,000 a year.

Conclusion: Linea Directa has a structurally advantaged cost position in a concentrated, high-barrier, compulsory market, and earns above-average returns under a competent but inward-facing management. These are good foundations with one external fragility (a mutual sets the market's prices) and one internal fragility (the reserve component of the margin cannot be seen).

Score: 62, set by the Rater. On the qualitative parts: the market is concentrated, compulsory and high-barrier, but its price discipline depends on a mutual price-setter (industry group 50). The cost advantage is real and structural, a 7-to-8-point expense gap that has held through a full cycle, but it is narrow, with low switching costs and softer advantages that are narrowing (competitive advantage 57). Management is a capable but inward-facing operator team (50). The financial profile is strong and clean (ROIC 22.4%, 92nd percentile; ROE 82nd percentile; no debt; no goodwill; growth needs only about EUR 35m a year, so new capital earns well above its cost). But predictability is low: the combined ratio took the pre-tax margin from 19.6% to a loss on a 9% revenue move, and reserve development is opaque. On balance it is above average but short of Carlsberg's franchise, and it sits between Carlsberg and Indutrade.

#4 Guidance conservatism and the record of delivery and upgrades

Management will meet its FY27 guidance, but FY27 consensus is about 6% too high, so the 2027 disappointment will come from the brokers, not from the company.

Guidance is verbal and covers outcomes only. Management guides to a CR in the "low 90s", an expense ratio below 20% over the medium term, more than 4 million customers, net profit above EUR 100m, and solvency not below 150% with about 180% as the dividend reference. It gives no guidance on premiums, EPS or payout.

Management raises guidance in small steps, after delivery and never ahead of it. The CR guidance moved from 94% to 95% (set late in 2024), to "92% is too good to be true" (Q3 25), to "comfortable with 92% to 93%" (February 2026) and to "low 90s" (April 2026), always with hedges on weather and technology costs. Delivery since FY24 has beaten every stated range: the CR was 94.7% in FY24, 92.6% in FY25, 91.7% in Q1 26 and 91.3% for nine months of 2026. The FY22 to FY23 record, however, was a severe miss (a CR of 96.3% and then 104.1%), in the one environment comparable to the one now developing.

Consensus has barely moved despite repeated beats, and the brokers share one margin assumption. The FactSet median of four to five brokers is consistent with a CR of about 91.2% in every year from FY26 to FY28. FY2027 consensus EPS has risen only 1.4% in twelve months despite repeated beats; meanwhile target prices fell 3% in the last month and the share of Buy ratings fell 10 points to 57%. The two Spanish Buy-rated brokers (JB Capital and Bestinver, both at EUR 0.110 of FY27 EPS) assume both more volume and a flat margin; UBS (EUR 0.101) is closest to us. The brokers' FY27 estimates span only EUR 0.100 to 0.110, because the brokers share one assumption rather than holding a range of views.

Inference: guidance is conservative for FY26 and neutral for FY27, while FY27 consensus is optimistic. For FY26, nine-month net income is already 78% of the full-year consensus, and a normal Q4 gives about EUR 105.5m, 2% above consensus. For FY27, our 92.0% CR sits inside the "low 90s" guidance, but consensus is about 6% to 7% too high. Management does not proactively manage expectations down; it is an honest tracker, so its upgrades rarely surprise. The record shows beats in stable conditions and misses in a claims-inflation turn, so the record cannot yet answer the test that 2027 sets.

So-what: in 2027 the gap will open between consensus and delivery, not between guidance and delivery. Management will meet its words while the brokers cut their numbers. That protects the company's credibility but does nothing for the share price between April and October 2027. The milestones (net profit above EUR 100m, 4 million customers in about Q2 27, and an expense ratio below 20%, now reachable in 2027) are all about to be met, so management will have to restate its ambitions.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market reads "low 90s" as confirmation of a 91% run-rate; we read it as a range whose upper half is where 2027 lands. The market's revisions are drifting down on the valuation measures (targets, ratings) while EPS edges up on beats. That pattern describes a market worried about a margin peak but not yet modelling the 2027 price-cost scissors.

Strongest counter-case. Q4 26 and Q1 27 print CRs at or below 91.5% with policy growth of 6% or more. That would validate the flat-CR assumption for two more quarters and push any consensus cuts beyond the window. We give that upside path a 25% probability. What would change our view: a Q1 27 motor loss ratio flat year on year alongside a derived written price increase of 3% or more.

Conclusion: guidance is conservative for FY26 and merely adequate for FY27, management upgrades only after the fact, and consensus sits 6% above our FY27 numbers. The expectation gap is therefore mildly unfavourable for the next nine months, and favourable only on the dividend.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. The company has beaten every stated combined-ratio range since FY24 and raised its words twice in 2026, always after delivery. But the record includes a severe FY22 to FY23 miss (combined ratio 104%) in the claims-inflation environment now recurring. Guidance is verbal and outcome-only, and the company does nothing to keep consensus conservative: FY27 consensus sits about 6% above deliverable, while the 'low 90s' guide will be met. This is an honest tracker, so it is placed above the Guidance (45) and Sell-side estimates (42) groups for the clean three-year beat record, near Entra, but below Renew.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Linea Directa has little leverage from revenue to profit and a great deal of leverage to its combined ratio, so profit grows with premiums in a normal year and swings by 9% per point of CR in an abnormal one.

Pricing power is relative and self-correcting, not absolute. Linea Directa can follow the market up within two to four quarters, at a churn cost of 3 to 5 points of policy growth: in 2023 to 2024 it made the largest increases in the sector, lost 4.5% of its customers, and grew customers 8.5% a year later. It cannot lead the market up; 2022 shows what happens when it tries to hold price into inflation. It currently chooses not to use the headroom it has, a 4-point price gap to the market with a CR 5 to 7 points better. In home insurance, pricing power is weaker: the average home premium has been falling under promotional pricing and is only now stabilising.

Operating leverage is small in the expense ratio and large in the CR, and it works in both directions. Roughly 55% of the cost base is fixed. That gives a gross gain of about 0.1 point of expense ratio for each 1% of premium growth, of which Linea Directa keeps 0.1 to 0.2 points a year net after reinvesting in price, marketing and technology (about EUR 2m to 3m of pre-tax profit a year). In 2026 it kept more, because the loss ratio did not need defending. The leverage that matters is underwriting leverage. At a 92% CR the technical margin is 8% of earned premium, so a 1-point move in the CR changes the technical result by about 12% and net profit by 9%. Revenue growth therefore does not produce outsized profit growth: profit grows roughly with revenue unless the CR moves, and the CR moves with claims cost and weather, not with volume.

Expense leverage

Underwriting leverage

Financial leverage: none. Linea Directa has EUR 1.6m of leases and no interest costs, refinancing needs or hybrid capital. The relevant gearing is insurance leverage: premiums are 2.7 times equity, which sets the 9%-per-point sensitivity of EPS to the CR. Interest rates act through solvency rather than earnings: 100 basis points cost about 10 points of solvency, and IFRS 17 discounting runs through other comprehensive income.

Cost scope: gradual gains, not a cost programme. Claims (about 71 points of the CR) can be reduced only through risk selection, fraud control and steering repairs into the company's network; the only disclosed figure for steered repairs fell from 71% (2021) to 50% (2022). Operating expenses are already lean. Marketing (about EUR 50m, or 4% to 5% of premiums) is the one large discretionary line, and technology and compliance costs are rising. The efficiency items that reach the profit and loss account by FY28 add about EUR 12m to 15m of pre-tax profit against FY26, and they are back-loaded: EUR 3m to 5m arrives in FY27 and most of the rest in FY28.

Feedback loops: one reinforcing loop against six balancing loops, so the system reverts to the mean. The reinforcing loop (lower cost, lower price, more volume, lower unit cost) drives growth above the market, and it is weakening as Linea Directa reprices and the price umbrella narrows. The balancing loops dominate the margin. New business runs 5 to 15 points worse than renewals, so slowing growth helps the loss ratio by about 0.25 point in FY27 to FY28. Growth consumes capital, so slowing growth releases the payout. Reserve prudence smooths reported results. The result is a CR held in a 91% to 92% band from both sides, growth converging on 5% to 7%, and lumpy EPS growth (FY27 about +1%, FY28 about +10%) that averages 7% to 8% a year.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market treats the falling expense ratio as the next earnings lever, because the CFO said that further CR improvement below 92% will come from expenses. We treat the expense ratio as a buffer: the leverage exists, but management's incentives spend it on volume when the CR is good and on holding the reported CR when it is not. The market also treats growth as the proof of the thesis. In our model, growth is worth about EUR 1m of net income per point of policy growth, and a great deal more through the multiple.

Strongest counter-case. The cost loop is stronger than modelled: fully online sales rise from 12%, AI absorbs service volumes, and the expense ratio falls below 19% by FY28 and stays there. That would add about EUR 12m of pre-tax profit (8%) above the model. What would change our view: two consecutive quarters other than Q1 with the expense ratio below 19.5% while policy growth holds above 5%.

Conclusion: the model has little revenue-to-profit leverage and a great deal of CR leverage, and the CR leverage is symmetric and externally driven. Earnings therefore grow at about the pace of premiums in a normal year and swing by 9% per point of CR in an abnormal one.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The structure has little upside gearing. About 55% of the expense base is fixed, but expenses are only about 20 points of a 92% combined ratio, so drop-through is about 0.1 point of ratio per 1% of growth, and most of that is reinvested in price. Pricing power is relative: the company follows the market up at a churn cost and cannot lead it. It has no financial leverage, cost-out is gradual (EUR 12m to 15m pre-tax by FY28) and the cost-price-volume loop is weakening. Forecast EPS grows about 1.1 times revenue against a typical 2 times. The large combined-ratio sensitivity is symmetric and external, so it is a risk (topic 9), not a gear. Profit grows roughly with revenue, which is the 25 to 50 level description, beside Bravida (36) and AQ Group (34).

The FY26 to FY28 profit bridge: the motor CR swings from the largest drag to a contributor. From FY26 to FY27, volume growth at the prior margin adds EUR 7.6m of pre-tax profit, but the motor CR (-5.2m) and the home CR (-3.2m) absorb most of that gain, so pre-tax profit rises only about EUR 1m. From FY27 to FY28, repricing earns through and the motor CR adds EUR 3.4m, so pre-tax profit rises about EUR 14m.

Against history: over the next four years, growth is higher than in the past but margins are not. The forecasts embed three regime changes:

  • Revenue growth of 5.5% to 10% a year, against 1.5% to 4.3% in FY19 to FY24, from share gains of 2 to 3 points a year on a market growing 4% to 6%.
  • A CR range-bound at 91% to 92%, against 96% to 104% in FY22 to FY24 and 86% to 90% before 2022.
  • A pre-tax margin of about 11%, far more stable than FY20 to FY23's swing from 19.6% to a loss, but about 5 points below FY19 to FY21.
Scope for double-digit growth: limited. EPS grows 23% in FY26 and 10% in FY28, and by single digits otherwise; the compound rate is 7.7% a year from FY25 to FY30. Double-digit EPS growth over the period would require either a CR nearer 90%, which the strategy spends on price, or capital return beyond the dividend, which solvency does not allow. The honest description is high-single-digit compounding with a 5% to 6% and rising dividend yield.

Credibility of the forecasts: FY26 is fixed, FY27 carries medium weight and leans down. The Financial Analyst's model reproduced H1 26 exactly and predicted the Q3 print inside every range it set in advance (nine-month net income EUR 80.4m, against an expected EUR 77m to 80m). FY26 net income is now fixed to within about EUR 3m. FY27 carries medium weight: the range is EUR 88m to 118m, and the probability-weighted figure is about EUR 103m (25% upside, 45% base, 30% downside). That weighted figure sits 3% below the base case, which measures the skew. FY28 to FY30 carry low-to-medium weight and lean slightly up, because health, repricing and the expense ratio could beat.

Where our view differs from the market's. On volume we are above consensus for FY27 (written premiums of EUR 1,316m against EUR 1,297m). On margin we are below consensus (a CR of 92.0% against an implied 91.2%). On dividends we are above consensus for FY26 and FY28. Our FY27 EPS is below the estimates of all five visible brokers.

Conclusion: the forecasts describe steady compounding with a 2027 air pocket, 2% above consensus this year and 5% to 7% below it for the next two years. Revenue is the most dependable line, and the CR is the only line that can move the answer by more than a few percent.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The 5% to 10% band gives C. I place it at the floor because the measure flatters the truth: FY26's +23% is the end of the margin recovery and is nine-months reported, and from FY26 onwards EPS compounds only about 4% a year to FY30, with a flat FY27. The pre-tax margin of about 11% stays 5 points below the pre-2022 past. The growth is all organic (no acquisitions) and better than the past only on volume.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Upgrades are confined to FY26, the dividend and the narrative over the next three months; from April 2027 the balance tips to FY27 cuts of 4% to 8%, which our numbers and management's words already contain.

Guidance: most likely met, with the payout the item most likely to rise. A raise is plausible only as a small change in words, such as "around 91% to 92%" or bringing the sub-20% expense-ratio target forward to 2027. The most likely moment is the FY26 results in late February, with a probability of about 30% at that event and 15% across the whole window. The item most likely to rise is the payout: we give a 50% probability to a step to 65% to 70% of profit at the FY26 or FY27 results. The solvency position (the 180% reference plus 3 points) rules out a buyback (under 10% probability).

Consensus: up into February 2027, then down to our numbers. The revisions should come in three phases:

WindowExpected revisionsBreadth
Now to February 2027FY26 EPS up 2% to 4% to about EUR 0.097 as the three brokers whose numbers date from July update them; FY27 EPS mechanically up 0% to 2%; dividend per share up towards EUR 0.058 to 0.060Positive: three or four of five brokers up
April to July 2027FY27 EPS down 3% to 6% and FY28 down 2% to 4%, as the Q1 27 and H1 27 results show the first year-on-year CR deterioration since 2023Negative: at least one more Hold rating
October 2027 to February 2028FY27 closes near EUR 0.098; FY28 rebased to EUR 0.108 to 0.112; FY29 initiated near our EUR 0.112

Over the whole window, we give FY27 consensus net income a 55% probability of being cut by more than 2%, a 30% probability of being held and a 15% probability of being raised; a raise needs the upside CR case plus faster volume. Small coverage magnifies any single change: each of the five brokers is 20% of breadth, and one Spanish broker moving its FY27 CR from 91% to 92% would cut the median by about 5% on its own. The signature to expect is EPS cuts and dividend upgrades at the same time, which is how a company whose payout rises as its growth slows looks to the market.

Narrative: the market's story is accurate but incomplete. The market's story is that Linea Directa is a cheap, over-capitalised direct insurer whose margin has peaked, whose growth is bought with low prices under a mutual that will not raise its own, whose earnings are shoppable, and which is small, illiquid and bank-owned. Two dynamics are known but not modelled: pricing of 2% against a 6% market, and a normal home CR of 90% to 91%; the CFO has stated both, but neither appears in FY27 consensus. Seven dynamics are articulated by nobody, and the table below sorts them into negatives and positives.

Inference and so-what: the case will look better in February 2027 than in July 2027. The unknown negative, the 2027 scissors, lands within six to twelve months and lands in the estimates. The unknown positives land either within three to four months and in the narrative (the Baremo, the dividend, the FY26 beat), or over three years (the plateau framing, the 2028 recovery). Net, the next six months bring narrative upgrades without estimate upgrades, and the following six months bring estimate downgrades that guidance accommodates.

Where our view differs from the market's. We expect consensus to come to our numbers, not our numbers to move to consensus. The direction of the next FY27 revision is one of the more predictable things in the case.

Strongest counter-case. The upside path (an FY27 CR of 91.0% to 91.3%) is a quarter of the distribution. Under that path consensus holds, the share of Buy ratings recovers, and the stock re-rates on a "margin durable through the Baremo test" story a year earlier than in our base case. What would change our view: the two readings named under #4 and #1, namely a flat Q1 27 motor loss ratio with a written price increase of 3% or more, and Mutua narrowing its freeze in March.

Conclusion: scope for upgrades is confined to FY26, the dividend and the narrative in the next three months. From April 2027 the balance tips to FY27 cuts of 4% to 8%, which are already in our numbers and inside management's words.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is most likely met rather than raised: raised 15%, reiterated 55%, lowered 30% across the window. Only the payout is likely to step up. Consensus, the next part, gets a small FY26 lift (+2% to 4%) by February and is then cut: FY27 by 4% to 8% from April to October 2027, with a cut of more than 2% at 55% against a raise at 15%. That is about -0.85 times the 7% revenue growth, partly offset by dividend upgrades. Narrative upgrades come only in the next three months (Baremo, dividend). Revisions lean negative within the 6 to 12 months, in line with the fourth-set group's 40 but lower, because the FY27 consensus gap is quantified and dated. It sits between TT Electronics and Indutrade.

The stock now trades as a small Spanish financial in a risk-off market, not on its own results. The retail P&C cohort sits at the bottom of its valuation history (Admiral 13.0x at the 9th percentile, Tryg 13.1x at the 4th, Sampo 13.5x at the 8th, Gjensidige 14.5x at the 18th), on the peaked-cycle and AI-agent stories (Morgan Stanley's Nordic notes in July and September, DNB Carnegie in October). Momentum is weak on every measure the dashboard reads, and strong on the one measure it does not read: operating delivery (35% profit growth, record customers, solvency rebuilt). Linea Directa is therefore not a momentum entry. The rising co-movement with the sector also means that sentiment shocks to the cohort, such as an AI-agent headline or a UK motor profit warning, will move the stock more than they did a year ago.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market's revision pattern (EPS nudged up by beats while targets and ratings drift down) is the right response to a margin peak. We think the peak framing is wrong, but we think the near-term direction of estimates is right, so we would not argue with the D ratings for the next two quarters.

Strongest counter-case. Thinly covered stocks whose returns are 74% idiosyncratic turn on single results. A February beat with a payout step and a benign Baremo could flip both D ratings within a quarter, as the late-2025 beats did. Conclusion: sell-side and technical momentum are both D, the cohort's momentum is poor and the stock's co-movement with the cohort is rising, so momentum gives no support today and none should be expected before the February 2027 results.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. The sell-side score is in the bottom fifth and relative strength sits at the median rather than above it, so neither measure is positive and the letter is D. The parts lean negative: buy share down 10 points to 57%, targets down 3%, the price below its 50-day average and only just above a 200-day average that has risen in 4 of 12 months, and the stock lagging its insurance basket (+4.6% against +12.4% over six months). The narrative is negative at cohort level. Spent but positive guidance momentum and a relative strength not in the bottom fifth place it in the lower-middle of the band.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple and trackable, but its FY27 outcome is skewed down, and the two drivers that matter most are the two the company does not disclose.

Simplicity: very high. Linea Directa has one country, one dominant line, one site, no debt, no minority interests, a statutory tax rate and a flat share count. The chain to net income is short: customers times average premium, earned with a six-month lag, times one minus the CR, plus the investment result, less EUR 7m of other items, times 0.75 after tax. Investors can see every link in that chain each quarter except two, the written price and the claims cost per policy, and those two links are exactly where the thesis lives.

The drivers are concentrated in the CR. The CR generates about 80% of the variance in FY27 earnings; volume generates about 10%, and investment income and expenses about 5% each. Within the CR, the motor price-cost gap is 55% of the variance, home weather 25%, health 10%, and reserving and large claims 10%.

The base case requires four things, and the first has never been done before.

  1. Linea Directa writes 2.5% to 3% of motor price increases from H1 27 while losing only growth, not customers, with Mutua's freeze still in place. The company has never done both at once.
  2. Home weather is no worse than normal.
  3. Reserves held at the 85th percentile prove adequate through a Baremo step of 3.3% to 3.5%, at a time when the prudent local incumbent, Mapfre, has just added 2 to 3 points to its own.
  4. The switch to the HNA health network lowers medical costs. That is unproven: so far only the health expense ratio has moved, not the health loss ratio.

The downside tail (about 5% probability) is a repeat of the 2022 configuration: claims inflation of 6% or more for two years, with Mutua's freeze in place and Linea Directa pricing late. That would give a CR of 96% to 98% and net income of EUR 55m to 70m.

Suddenness and trackability: the company gives no early warning, but the external drivers are dated and public. Severity steps and weather hit results within a quarter, and investors learn of them only from the results. Linea Directa discloses no written price, claims frequency, claims severity, retention or reserve development, and its calls are led by the CFO without public questions. The external drivers are more visible. The Baremo is set by formula and published in December. Mapfre discloses its average premium, fleet and reserving quarterly, and is the best proxy for the market. Mutua announces its tariff policy publicly, next in March 2027. The Q1 27 results in late April are the single most informative event of the window, because Q1 27 is the first quarter with both the 2027 Baremo and the HNA network.

Share-price risks: the fundamental ones are large and dated; the sentiment ones are more frequent.

Fundamental

  • A 1-point CR miss is 9% of EPS and, at a 10x to 11x multiple, 10% to 18% of the share price.
  • The downside case is -33% to -37%.

Sentiment

  • A Bankinter placement of its 17.4% (about EUR 230m against about USD 1.2m traded a day) would be a 5% to 10% day.
  • An AI-agent or autonomous-vehicle de-rating of the cohort (Admiral's 45% relative de-rating; the Nordics' -6.9% in three months).
  • A Mutua headline, or a UK motor profit warning read across to Spain.
  • A credibility event (a restatement or regulatory finding), given rising control weaknesses.
  • A risk-off squeeze on small, illiquid names.

Cushions

  • A 4.7% to 5.1% yield on our FY26 to FY27 dividends.
  • A 52-week low of EUR 1.04.
  • Controlling shareholders who have been buying.
  • A multiple already at the 8th to 10th percentile, which limits the downside from the multiple alone to about 10% to 15%.

Precedents: Linea Directa sits after the repricing peak, with a stable margin, which historically returns earnings plus dividends until a catalyst arrives.

  • Spanish motor CRs ran between 90% and 105% from 2014 to 2023. Once Linea Directa's written price fell below claims inflation, its motor loss ratio rose 8.3 points in 2022 and its motor CR a further 9.5 points in 2023, and group pre-tax profit swung by EUR 186m on revenue that moved 9%.
  • The 2016 Baremo reform cost Linea Directa about 190 basis points of CR, at a 90% CR, while the market ran at 100%. That episode is the better precedent for a 3.5% Baremo step taken from a strong position.
  • Elsewhere: Direct Line priced late in 2022 (CR 103%, dividend cancelled, later sold to Aviva); Sabre shrank 14% in 2025 to protect its margin and then had its estimates cut 5% to 7% in October 2026; UK motor insurers cut rates in 2025 and expect losses in 2026; Admiral held its margins through 2010 to 2020 with a 10-point cost gap and most risk ceded to reinsurers.
  • The motor cycle's rule of thumb is that a year of rate increases above claims inflation gives about six quarters of rising earned margin, and that investors should leave a market whose repricing has peaked. That rule places Linea Directa after the peak.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market prices the risk in the multiple and not in the estimates; we price the risk in the estimates (FY27 -6%) and think the multiple is roughly right. The market's downside case anchors on 2023. Ours is bounded by a Baremo step one-third the size, a starting CR 13 points better, an expense buffer the company did not have in 2022, and a market already raising prices. Reserves are the one area where we have less comfort than the market appears to have: the market does not discuss reserves at all.

Strongest counter-case to our risk framing. The risks are more symmetric than we allow: Mutua is one inflation step from its CR ceiling, parts inflation could fade with energy prices, and the 2025 reserve surplus could repeat. What would change our view: March 2027 accounts showing a 2026 run-off surplus of the 2025 size with the 85th-percentile risk adjustment unchanged. That would mean the book is better reserved than the percentile suggests.

Conclusion: the case is simple, concentrated and trackable one quarter in arrears. Its FY27 outcome is negatively skewed, but the downside is dated, bounded and about one-fifth the amplitude of 2022 to 2023. Sentiment risks are more frequent than the fundamental ones, and Linea Directa's size, small free float and rising co-movement with a de-rated cohort amplify them.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The case is very simple and trackable: one country, one dominant line, no debt, mechanical below underwriting, and the external drivers are dated (Baremo on 15 December, Mutua in March). But the FY27 EPS cone is about -17% to +11% and negatively skewed. One combined-ratio point is 9% of EPS. An unseen reserve lever is worth -18% to -27% of EPS, and the memo gives a 30% chance to a -30% share-price case. Sentiment risks are frequent (a Bankinter placement on a thin float, AI-agent read-across from the cohort). It is the levels' 50 profile (simple mechanism, range about 15% either way), so I set it below the Risks groups' 58 to 60, weighing the fat dated tail and the reserve opacity more heavily, between NKT and IMCD.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The dashboard's rule says Bottoming. We agree on the price and the multiple, and disagree on the estimates. The dashboard's rule reads the multiple at the 10th percentile, technical and sell-side momentum both at D, and valuation at A.

  • The multiple is bottoming. The stock has been bottoming since December 2025 (11.0x), after de-rating from 14.5x in May 2025 while earnings rose by more than 30%. The multiple has not broken the 11x floor in eleven months, and the 52-week low held in a risk-off market.
  • The estimates are stalling. The recovery that drove the FY24 to FY26 upgrades is complete. Growth is decelerating gently: written premium growth slowed from +10.2% in Q1 to +8.3% in Q3, and net customer additions fell from 70,000 to 60,000 to 40,000 by quarter. The share of Buy ratings is falling, and the next revisions to FY27 are down.
  • The narrative sits between stalling and bottoming. "Margin peak" and "mutual price war" are stalling stories, but the negatives are fully known and in the price.

What moves the stock to Turning Up, and when. Three routes exist, in order of probability. The first is proof that the CR holds in the low 90s through the 2027 Baremo and the January renewal round, visible in the Q1 27 results (late April) and confirmed at H1 27 (late July). The second is a capital-policy step in February, and the third a Mutua retreat in March. The first route is the one that history says re-rates a motor insurer after its repricing peak (Admiral, 2010 to 2020), and it is six to nine months away. If instead the Q1 27 motor loss ratio rises by more than 1.5 points, the phase becomes Stalling, consensus falls 15% to 20%, and the multiple tests the 9.4x to 10x trough.

Where our view differs from the market's. The dashboard reads Bottoming from the multiple and momentum alone. We would call the stock "Bottoming on price, Stalling on estimates", a common and awkward combination: the cheapness is real, but the catalyst that converts it into a re-rating is a test still to be sat, and the estimates must fall before they can rise.

Strongest counter-case. The stock is already Turning Up: it has held EUR 1.1 to 1.3 for a year, FY26 beats are coming, the Baremo relief is dated, and the market's habit of trading this stock on its own results (74% idiosyncratic) means February could mark the turn. What would change our view: FY26 results that deliver both a payout range of 70% or more and 2027 guidance words tighter than "low 90s".

Conclusion: the stock is Bottoming on the multiple and the price and Stalling on earnings momentum. The turn up depends on passing the April-to-July 2027 margin test, or on a capital or competitor catalyst that is plausible but unsignalled.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'Bottoming on price, Stalling on estimates'. The multiple has held at the 10th percentile for eleven months and the 52-week low held, but the recovery that drove upgrades is complete. Net additions are slowing (70k, 60k, 40k by quarter), the buy share is falling, and FY27 estimates must fall 4% to 8% before the April-to-July 2027 margin test can turn the phase up. Less attractive than CVS's credible Bottoming with slightly negative revisions, it is more attractive than National Grid's clean Stalling, because the price already discounts the known negatives.

#11 The fair multiple

12.38x is the right multiple today, and because the stock already trades there on our earnings, the multiple is neither the risk nor the reward in the base case.

The guideline: 12.38x two-year-forward earnings. Viewforth's rule sets the guideline for a Bottoming stock at the 30th percentile of the stock's ten-year range. The guideline is 10% above the 11.28x the market pays on consensus earnings (6 November 2026) and 1.5% above the 12.2x it pays on our earnings.

The multiple's history: the 2023 to 2024 spikes reflect collapsed earnings, not a richer rating. Linea Directa listed in April 2021 at 15.8x and EUR 1.5 a share. It de-rated through the 2022 shock to a trough of 9.7x in September 2022 (the five-year weekly low is 9.44x). The multiple spiked to 15x to 16x in 2023 and 2024 only because earnings had collapsed, while the share price was EUR 0.7 to 0.9. It traded at 13.4x to 14.9x through H1 25 as earnings recovered, and then de-rated to 11x to 12x from October 2025 while earnings kept rising. In the ten-year distribution, the 10th percentile is 11.0x, the median 13.4x, the 75th percentile 14.9x and the 90th percentile 16.4x. The current 11.3x falls in what the dashboard labels the "crash" band.

Our view: 12.4x is fair, and we would not argue for more today. Four reasons support that view:

  1. The stock is past the repricing peak with a stable margin. That is the phase in which the sector pays low multiples until margin durability is proved, and the proof is six to nine months away.
  2. FY27 to FY28 consensus will be cut by 4% to 8%, so a multiple struck on today's consensus overstates the cheapness by about a turn: 11.3x on consensus is 12.2x on our numbers.
  3. The retail P&C cohort trades at 12.9x to 14.5x, at the bottom of its own ranges. A 12.4x multiple asks Linea Directa only to close part of its discount to a cohort that is itself depressed; it does not require the cohort to recover.
  4. Linea Directa has not used its own catalysts for closing the discount: disclosure, investor access and capital policy.

Against that, the multiple justified by fundamentals is higher. A 23% ROE growing 4% to 5% a year at a 9% to 10% cost of equity supports about 3.2 to 4.5 times book value, or roughly 14x to 19x current earnings; on a normalised CR of 92% to 93%, it supports about 12x to 14x. The gap between 12.4x and those levels is the price of the reserve opacity, the mutual competitor next door, the small free float and the memory of 2023.

Delivery case

If the CR holds through 2027 and the payout reaches 70%, the stock enters a delivery phase. The cohort's 13x to 13.5x then becomes the right reference, worth +5% to +10% from the multiple alone.

Stalling case

If the CR stalls at 93% to 94%, the market will pay 10x to 11x on reduced earnings, as it did in 2022 and December 2025.

Where our view differs from the market's. The market pays 11.3x because it believes the margin has peaked and the earnings are shoppable. We believe the margin is a plateau below the company's history, and that competitors cannot shop the volume away while the cost gap holds; that argues for 13x or more in time. But we also believe the market is right about the next two revisions, which argues for 12.4x now. We land on the guideline.

Strongest counter-case: a takeover bid. Linea Directa is the only listed pure direct insurer in Spain and trades at a 10th-percentile multiple, in a sector that has paid 17 times earnings (Mapfre for Safety) and has bought a direct motor insurer (Aviva for Direct Line). A bid would need the support of the two shareholder blocks, so it is optionality rather than a base case, but it caps how far the multiple should be allowed to fall. What would change our view: a re-rating of the cohort (the AI-agent and peaked-cycle stories fading), or Linea Directa closing its discount with a capital policy and better disclosure. Either would move the fair multiple towards the ten-year median of 13.4x.

Conclusion: 12.38x is the right multiple for a stock whose margin durability is unproved and whose estimates are about to fall. Because the stock already trades at 12.38x on our earnings, the multiple is neither the risk nor the reward in the base case.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. The raw readings are cheap on both measures (A), but I move the letter to B because part of the cheapness is a measurement artefact. The 'ten-year' range is five years since the 2021 listing and is inflated by the 15x-to-16x multiples on collapsed 2023-24 earnings, which also lift the 1.70x average cohort premium. On the memo's earnings, 6% below an unrebased consensus, the stock is at 12.2x, about the 25th to 30th percentile (neutral), and at its guideline fair multiple. Against the cohort it still trades cheap. I place it in the middle of B because a 23% ROE debt-free compounder still warrants more than the market pays.

#12 Total shareholder return

The base return is earnings plus dividends with almost nothing from the multiple: +21.6% to December 2027, but about +10% once weighted for the skew, with a dated downside of about -30%.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (share price EUR 1.23 on 25 October 2026):

To 30-Jun-29 (the three-year column)+33.6%+11.5%EUR 1.64+14.9%+1.6%+16.8%

The multiple and earnings parts multiply, and the dividends add. The earnings part comes from rolling the two-year-forward EPS forward: from about EUR 0.101 today (a blend of FY27 and FY28) to about EUR 0.112 at December 2027 (FY29) and about EUR 0.118 at June 2029 (a blend of FY30 and FY31). The implied share price is about EUR 1.39 at December 2027 and about EUR 1.46 at June 2029, with EUR 0.11 and EUR 0.18 of cumulative dividends on top. The December 2027 price is close to the brokers' mean target of EUR 1.41, but it is reached on lower earnings and a higher multiple than the brokers use.

What drives the return, in order of size.

  1. Earnings: 11 of the 21.6 points. The two-year-forward roll jumps over the flat FY27 and captures the FY28 recovery, so the earnings contribution to December 2027 is larger than FY27's +1% EPS growth suggests. The return is therefore back-loaded to the period after the H1 27 results, when the market can see FY28.
  2. Dividends: 8.8 of the 21.6 points, and 14.9 of the 33.6 points. Dividends are 40% to 45% of the three-year return. The yield on our dividends is 4.7% (FY26), 5.1% (FY27) and 6.1% (FY28), and the rising payout is itself a product of slowing growth.
  3. The multiple: 1.6 points, because on our earnings the stock already trades at the guideline. Any larger re-rating is upside to the model, not part of it.

The range around the model's return: skew and path cut the expected return to about +10%.

  • Downside case (FY27 CR 93.8%, EPS EUR 0.082, multiple 9.5x to 10x): a share price of EUR 0.78 to 0.82 plus about EUR 0.06 of dividends, a total return of about -30% to the end of 2027.
  • Upside case (FY27 CR 91.0%, FY27 EPS EUR 0.106, two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 0.12 at December 2027, cohort multiple of 13x): a share price of about EUR 1.56 plus EUR 0.11 of dividends, about +36%.
  • Probability-weighted at 25% upside, 45% base and 30% downside (0.25 x 36 + 0.45 x 21.6 + 0.30 x -30), the expected 14-month return is roughly +10%, below the model's +21.6% because of the skew and the path.
The path: the return is not earned evenly, and the choice is when to buy. The window to February 2027 is supportive (FY26 beat, dividend, Baremo, solvency uplift). April to October 2027 is adverse (CR deterioration, consensus cuts, Mutua). The recovery becomes visible from the H1 27 results and is priced through 2028. A buyer today earns the dividends through the air pocket but carries the drawdown risk of the consensus cuts. A buyer after the Q1 27 or H1 27 results gives up a quarter or two of dividend yield, and perhaps a February rally, in exchange for a cleaner read on judgements 1 to 3.

Where our view differs from the market's. The brokers' 15% upside to their mean target rests on earnings 6% to 12% above ours at a lower multiple. Our return rests on lower earnings, a higher dividend and a multiple the stock already carries. Both routes land near EUR 1.4 a share for different reasons, which tells us the stock is not mispriced on the destination. It is mispriced, mildly and negatively, on the path.

Strongest counter-case. The model's return understates the case, because it allows no re-rating from the cohort's depressed level and no capital return beyond a 70% payout. A payout policy and a disclosure step could add 5 to 10 points from the multiple within the 18 months. What would change our view: the February 2027 capital statement.

Conclusion: the model's +21.6% to December 2027 and +33.6% to June 2029 are an earnings-plus-dividend return with almost nothing from the multiple, back-loaded to after the 2027 margin test. The probability-weighted 14-month return is nearer +10%, and the downside case of about -30% is dated and bounded.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. About +10% to +12% sits at the bottom of the C band, about 52 on the scale. It is mostly dividends (8.8 points) and earnings, with almost nothing from the multiple. The three-year base check (+33.6%) supports it, but the lower tail is fat and dated (a 30% chance of about -30% through the April-to-October 2027 consensus cuts), which holds it near the floor of the band.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

The business

Good: the lowest-cost personal-lines insurer in Spain, with high returns and no debt

The price

Cheap: near the bottom of its own history and of a depressed cohort

The timing

A problem: a flat FY27 that consensus has not yet modelled

Linea Directa is a good business at a cheap price with a timing problem. The business is Spain's lowest-cost personal-lines insurer. It shares a structural 7-to-8-point expense advantage with customers to take market share at the best margin in its market, and it earns a 23% to 25% ROE with no debt, a short-tail book and a capital position that lets it pay out 60% to 70% of profit while growing 7% a year. The price is 11.3x consensus earnings and 12.2x our earnings, at the 10th percentile of the stock's own history, alongside a retail P&C cohort that is also at its lows, with a 4.7% dividend yield rising to 6%. The timing problem is that the margin recovery is over: 2026's deliberately low pricing earns through in 2027 against 3.5% to 4.5% claims-cost growth, home weather reverts, and FY27 earnings are flat and about 6% below a consensus that will discover the gap between April and July 2027. Management's guidance words accommodate that flat year; the brokers' numbers do not.

Why the case deserves Richard's attention now: the market misreads four things in the next four months. The market carries the 2027 Baremo as an open fear, when the pension formula has already fixed it at about 3.3% to 3.5%. The market calls a 91% to 92% CR a peak, when the company's own history was 86% to 88%. The market does not model the payout step that slowing growth makes affordable. And the market has not connected Mapfre's and AXA's 2027 growth plans to the medium-term soft-market risk, which is the risk we would worry about most for 2028 to 2029.

Why the case is one to stage rather than to take whole: the arithmetic is asymmetric. One point of CR is 9% of EPS, the downside case sits further from the base than the upside case, the reserve component of the margin cannot be seen, and the proof that would turn a bottoming multiple into a rising one is the Q1 27 result in late April 2027.

What a holder earns, and what would change the skew. The model's return of +21.6% to December 2027 is a fair statement of what a holder earns if the base case lands: 11 points from earnings growth (which jumps over the flat year), 9 points from dividends and almost nothing from re-rating. The unusually positive skew Richard looks for is not present today. It would appear if February brings a payout policy of 70% or more, if March brings a Mutua retreat, or if April shows the loss ratio holding with a 3% written price. Each is plausible, none is in the price, and all three are dated.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 48, set by the Rater. The input forces nearly cancel: external is slightly negative (48), with the umbrella offset by claims inflation and an earlier soft market, and internal is gently positive but narrowing (54). The financial output is weak, at C at the band floor with about 4% a year from FY26 and a flat FY27. So there is no material net change, and profits grow below the typical company's rate, which puts it a touch below 50, in line with the memo's C.

Foundations' Robustness: 66, set by the Rater. Quality (62) rests on a compulsory, concentrated, high-barrier market with non-discretionary demand and a cost advantage that has survived a full cycle, plus top-decile returns, no debt and clean earnings. Unlike CVS (Richard 80), its margins are not stable: they swung to a loss in 2023. Reserves are opaque, the business is a single line, and a mutual sets prices. The delivery record (54) is honest but includes that miss, so it sits above Judges Scientific's 60 but below the memo's B.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 52, set by the Rater. The best fit is a cause for concern clearing (margin durability through the 2027 inflation step under Mutua's freeze) in a medium-to-high-quality, low-capital business. The shape is clean, but the setup's key element, the concern clearing, is absent today: the business faces a real margin air pocket in 2027, and the test is not yet sat. So it fits in kind while missing one important element, below Richard's 65 to 75 for a major cause for concern that is clearing (CVS).

Case Riskiness: 50, set by the Rater. Risk and simplicity (50): the case is simple, debt-free, trackable and on a low multiple with a 5% yield cushion. Unlike CVS's 'paper cuts', its risks are concentrated in one negatively skewed ratio worth 9% of EPS per point, an opaque reserve lever, and a dated -30% tail with a 30% probability. Management does nothing to keep FY27 consensus conservative, and sentiment risk is amplified by float and the cohort, so it sits at the middle, in line with the memo's C.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
